title: Diabetic Kidney Disease: Confirm Chronicity and Layer Kidney-Protective Therapy
bottomLine: Diabetic kidney disease is defined by persistent albuminuria and/or reduced eGFR in the appropriate clinical context, not one abnormal urine or creatinine value. Confirm chronicity, control blood pressure and glycemia, use kidney-protective RAAS/SGLT2/GLP-1/nsMRA therapy when indicated, and refer atypical or rapidly progressive disease rather than assuming every CKD finding in diabetes is diabetic nephropathy.
recognize: Albuminuria may precede eGFR decline, but some patients have reduced eGFR without substantial albuminuria.
A rapid eGFR decline, active urine sediment, abrupt heavy proteinuria, systemic features or absence of expected diabetic context raises concern for non-diabetic kidney disease.
differentiate: Transient albuminuria can occur with exercise, fever, infection, marked hyperglycemia or uncontrolled blood pressure and must not be labelled chronic disease from one sample.
Diabetic kidney disease can coexist with another glomerular, ischemic or obstructive process.
assessment: Assess diabetes duration/control, BP, cardiovascular disease/HF, volume status, medications including NSAIDs, smoking, urinary symptoms, retinopathy context and access/adherence.
Review orthostasis, frailty and hypoglycemia because overaggressive BP/glycemic treatment can cause harm in advanced disease.
workup: Use urine ACR and serum creatinine/eGFR, repeating abnormalities to establish persistent CKD when the patient is stable.
Use urinalysis/sediment, renal imaging and nephrology workup when atypical features suggest another cause.
management: Use RAAS inhibition for appropriate albuminuric/hypertensive disease and SGLT2 inhibition for eligible patients with kidney benefit; add GLP-1RA and/or nsMRA where current Diabetes Canada criteria and patient factors support them.
Treat cardiovascular risk, smoking, glycemia and BP together rather than focusing only on ACR.
medicationSafety: Monitor potassium, renal function and BP after clinically meaningful RAAS/nsMRA changes and during acute illness.

SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/perioperative counselling and recognition of euglycemic DKA/volume risks; do not discontinue kidney-protective therapy reflexively for a small expected early eGFR change without clinical review.
redFlags: Active urine sediment or systemic nephritis features
counselling: Explain that kidney protection often uses medications for organ benefit even when glucose or BP already looks reasonably controlled.
Teach NSAID avoidance and sick-day medication plans appropriate to the regimen.
followUp: Trend ACR/eGFR, potassium, BP and treatment tolerance at intervals matched to CKD stage/risk; use KFRE and nephrology referral where appropriate.
examTrap: Calling one elevated urine ACR 'diabetic nephropathy' without confirming persistence or considering a different kidney disease when the presentation is atypical.
oneLinePearl: Confirm diabetic CKD, then layer kidney-protective therapy while watching for signs it is not actually diabetic kidney disease.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada 2025 Chronic Kidney Disease in Diabetes update

title: Hypertensive Kidney Disease: Control Pressure Without Missing Another Cause
bottomLine: Chronic hypertension can contribute to CKD, but 'hypertensive nephrosclerosis' should not become a label for every patient with high BP and low eGFR. Confirm chronicity, quantify albuminuria, assess vascular/systemic clues, control BP using kidney-protective therapy, and investigate discordant heavy proteinuria, active sediment or rapid decline.
recognize: Long-standing hypertension, vascular disease and gradually declining kidney function with modest proteinuria can fit hypertensive kidney disease.
Severe/resistant hypertension can be both cause and consequence of kidney disease.
differentiate: Heavy proteinuria, active urine sediment, abrupt kidney decline or systemic inflammatory features are not classic simple hypertensive nephrosclerosis and require another differential.
Renovascular disease, primary glomerular disease and diabetic kidney disease can coexist with hypertension.
assessment: Review standardized BP/home readings, duration/severity, medications/adherence, NSAIDs/decongestants/stimulants, orthostasis, vascular disease, edema and secondary-hypertension clues.
workup: Use creatinine/eGFR, ACR, urinalysis and electrolytes; pursue imaging/secondary-cause testing only when the clinical pattern warrants it.
Do not diagnose the cause from kidney size or one eGFR value alone.
management: Use evidence-based BP control with RAAS blockade when albuminuria/other indications support it and integrate sodium, smoking, cardiovascular and diabetes management.
Individualize BP targets to tolerability, frailty, orthostasis and comorbidity rather than pursuing one number at any cost.
medicationSafety: Monitor creatinine/eGFR and potassium after RAAS blockade changes; review diuretic-related volume/electrolyte effects.
Avoid chronic NSAIDs in CKD/hypertension when possible because they can worsen BP, perfusion and kidney function.
counselling: Teach validated home BP technique, medication adherence and avoidance of nephrotoxic OTC drugs.
followUp: Trend BP, eGFR, ACR and electrolytes; refer uncertain/rapidly progressive disease rather than repeatedly renewing a presumed-cause label.
examTrap: Assuming hypertension explains CKD despite nephrotic-range proteinuria and hematuria that point toward glomerular disease.
oneLinePearl: Hypertension can injure kidneys, but the kidney pattern still has to fit.
sourceBasis: Canadian CKD and hypertension practice resources

title: CKD Electrolytes: Treat the Cause, the ECG Risk, and the Volume Context
bottomLine: Advanced CKD changes potassium, sodium, bicarbonate, phosphate, magnesium and medication handling. Prioritize dangerous hyperkalemia/ECG change and symptomatic electrolyte abnormalities, correct reversible drugs/diet/volume issues, and avoid reflexively stopping all kidney-protective therapy without an effort to manage the complication.
recognize: Hyperkalemia risk rises with declining GFR, RAAS blockers/nsMRA, potassium supplements, acidosis, diabetes and tissue injury.
Dilutional hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis and phosphate retention often reflect volume and advanced-kidney physiology rather than isolated dietary problems.
differentiate: Pseudohyperkalemia from hemolysis/thrombocytosis differs from true dangerous hyperkalemia, but ECG instability must be treated immediately while confirming the value.
A mild chronic abnormality in stable CKD differs from an acute rapid change with arrhythmia, weakness or neurologic symptoms.
assessment: Assess ECG/symptoms when potassium is significant, volume status, intake, urine output, diarrhea/vomiting, medications/supplements, dialysis status and recent renal-function change.
workup: Repeat questionable critical values promptly without delaying treatment of a clinically dangerous presentation; use bicarbonate/acid-base, magnesium, calcium/phosphate and renal trend according to the problem.
management: Dangerous hyperkalemia requires membrane stabilization when indicated, intracellular shift and potassium removal through the appropriate acute-care pathway.
For chronic recurrent hyperkalemia, review diet/constipation/acidosis/medications and consider potassium-lowering strategies so beneficial RAAS therapy can sometimes continue under monitoring.
medicationSafety: Avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes/supplements unless specifically indicated.
Renal impairment increases toxicity from magnesium-containing products and many renally cleared drugs; medication reconciliation is central.
redFlags: Dialysis patient with missed treatment plus cardiopulmonary symptoms
counselling: Teach individualized—not blanket—diet advice and which OTC supplements/salt substitutes are unsafe.
Provide a sick-day/urgent-care plan for worsening kidney function or missed dialysis.
followUp: Recheck electrolytes after medication/diet/volume changes at intervals matched to severity and renal function.
examTrap: Permanently stopping all RAAS therapy after mild chronic hyperkalemia without addressing reversible contributors or considering strategies that preserve kidney/cardiovascular benefit.
oneLinePearl: In CKD, manage the electrolyte problem while protecting the therapies that protect the kidney when safely possible.

title: Anemia of CKD: Prove the Cause Before ESA Therapy
bottomLine: Anemia in CKD is often multifactorial. Confirm iron status and alternative causes before attributing it to erythropoietin deficiency; correct iron deficiency and bleeding when present, use ESA selectively to reduce clinically important anemia/transfusion burden, and do not normalize hemoglobin because higher ESA targets can increase harm.
recognize: CKD anemia is usually normocytic but iron deficiency, inflammation, B12/folate deficiency, hemolysis or occult blood loss can change the pattern.
Dialysis and frequent blood loss/phlebotomy can increase iron requirements.
differentiate: A low hemoglobin in CKD is not automatically an ESA indication.
Acute bleeding/hemolysis is managed as an acute anemia syndrome rather than by increasing ESA dose.
assessment: Assess fatigue/dyspnea, bleeding, dialysis, nutrition, inflammation/infection, medications, transfusion history and malignancy/thrombotic risk.
workup: Use CBC/indices, ferritin and transferrin-saturation/iron assessment plus B12/folate/retic or other tests as clinically indicated.
Look for occult blood loss or another cause when the severity/pattern is disproportionate to kidney disease.
management: Replace iron using oral or IV strategy according to CKD stage, deficiency, tolerance and dialysis context.

ESA initiation/targeting is individualized and generally conservative; Choosing Wisely Canada recommends against initiating ESA simply to normalize hemoglobin and specifically advises not initiating in asymptomatic CKD patients when hemoglobin is already at/above 100 g/L.
medicationSafety: ESA overtreatment increases cardiovascular/thrombotic risk and hypertension; dose/target should be conservative and individualized.
IV iron requires monitoring for infusion reactions and avoidance during selected active infection contexts according to specialty guidance.
counselling: Explain that the goal of CKD anemia therapy is symptom/transfusion reduction and safe function—not a 'normal' hemoglobin at any cost.
followUp: Trend hemoglobin, iron indices, BP and treatment response; reassess the diagnosis when response is poor.
examTrap: Starting or escalating ESA solely to normalize hemoglobin in a stable CKD patient without first checking iron deficiency or other anemia causes.
oneLinePearl: CKD anemia treatment aims for safety and symptoms—not normal-range hemoglobin.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Nephrology recommendations updated 2025

title: CKD Mineral-Bone Disorder: Read Calcium, Phosphate, PTH, and Bone Risk Together
bottomLine: CKD-MBD is a disorder of phosphate/calcium/PTH/vitamin-D/bone/vascular physiology, not 'osteoporosis with renal disease.' Interpret trends and CKD stage together, avoid indiscriminate calcium/vitamin-D/phosphate-binder use, and involve nephrology when biochemical abnormalities, fracture risk or advanced CKD make treatment complex.
recognize: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol drive secondary hyperparathyroidism as CKD advances.
Both high and overly suppressed PTH states can be harmful; a single PTH result should not drive aggressive therapy without stage/trend context.
differentiate: Primary hyperparathyroidism, vitamin-D deficiency, osteoporosis and CKD-MBD can overlap but have different biochemical patterns/treatments.
Serum calcium may be normal despite substantial CKD-MBD.
assessment: Review CKD stage/trend, fractures/bone pain, calcium/phosphate/vitamin-D intake/supplements, dialysis, pruritus, vascular calcification risk and relevant medications.
workup: Trend calcium, phosphate, PTH, alkaline phosphatase and vitamin-D testing when clinically indicated by stage/treatment; assess fracture risk/BMD selectively.
Avoid acting on one isolated PTH or phosphate result when the longitudinal pattern is more informative.
management: Control phosphate exposure and use binders/vitamin-D-related therapy according to stage, trends and nephrology guidance.
Treat osteoporosis/fracture risk with renal-function/CKD-MBD context because standard osteoporosis drugs may require modification in advanced CKD.
medicationSafety: Excess calcium-based binder/supplement exposure can contribute to hypercalcemia/vascular calcification.
Active vitamin-D analogues/calcimimetics can produce calcium disturbances and require monitored specialty use.
counselling: Explain why kidney-related bone disease is about mineral/hormone balance as well as bone density and why diet advice is individualized.
followUp: Track biochemical trends and treatment effects according to CKD stage/modalities; coordinate nephrology for advanced disease.
examTrap: Treating a single elevated PTH in CKD as primary hyperparathyroidism without considering phosphate retention and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
oneLinePearl: CKD-MBD is a trend-and-stage disorder, not one abnormal PTH value.
sourceBasis: Kidney Foundation of Canada CKD education

title: Dialysis: Start for Clinical Indications, Prepare Before Crisis
bottomLine: Chronic dialysis should not begin solely because eGFR crosses a number. Prepare early for kidney replacement/supportive-care options, but initiate dialysis when symptoms or refractory complications of kidney failure justify it—such as uncontrollable volume, potassium/acidosis, uremic complications or other clinical indications—through shared decision-making.
recognize: Advanced CKD planning should begin before emergency kidney failure so access, home modalities, transplant evaluation and conservative kidney management can be considered.
Uremic symptoms can include anorexia/nausea, pruritus, cognitive/pericardial/neurologic manifestations and progressive functional decline, but each symptom still needs a differential.
differentiate: A low eGFR in an otherwise stable asymptomatic patient is not by itself an automatic dialysis start.
Acute dialysis indications in AKI and elective chronic kidney-failure planning overlap in physiology but differ in timing/context.
assessment: Assess volume/BP, potassium/acidosis, nutrition/weight, cognition, nausea/appetite, pruritus, pericarditic/neurologic symptoms, medication burden, goals, frailty and support/home circumstances.
workup: Trend renal function, electrolytes/acid-base, volume/nutrition and complication burden; use nephrology kidney-failure risk/planning tools rather than one creatinine/eGFR threshold.
Plan vascular/peritoneal access and transplant assessment early enough to avoid emergency catheter starts when possible.
management: Discuss hemodialysis, peritoneal/home options, transplant and active conservative kidney management based on goals and clinical suitability.
Start dialysis for clinical indications/refractory complications through nephrology rather than pre-emptively from laboratory stage alone.
medicationSafety: Medication doses and dialyzability change with kidney failure/dialysis and must be reviewed before/after initiation.
Avoid unnecessary PICC/vascular injury in advanced CKD when future dialysis access is a concern.
counselling: Explain dialysis as one kidney-failure treatment option, not an inevitable calendar date, and discuss conservative care as active care when it fits the person's goals.
followUp: Ensure modality/access/transplant/supportive-care planning is closed-loop and not deferred until an emergency hospitalization.
examTrap: Starting chronic dialysis in a stable asymptomatic stage-5 CKD patient solely because eGFR falls below a memorized cutoff.
oneLinePearl: Prepare early for dialysis; start it for the patient's clinical need, not the eGFR alone.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Nephrology recommendations updated 2025
Kidney Foundation of Canada kidney-failure treatment options

title: Kidney Transplant Follow-Up: Protect the Graft, Watch the Immunosuppression
bottomLine: A kidney transplant recipient remains chronically immunosuppressed with ongoing risks of rejection, infection, medication toxicity, malignancy and cardiovascular/metabolic disease. Do not adjust transplant immunosuppression casually; recognize graft dysfunction/infection early and coordinate promptly with the transplant program.
recognize: Creatinine rise may reflect rejection, dehydration, obstruction, infection, drug toxicity or recurrent disease; symptoms can be minimal.
Immunosuppression increases risk of opportunistic infection and malignancy, while calcineurin inhibitors and steroids can worsen BP, diabetes, lipids and kidney function.
differentiate: A positive urine culture or fever may represent more serious infection in an immunosuppressed recipient than in a routine outpatient.
Medication nonadherence or interaction-induced low immunosuppressant exposure can precipitate rejection; high exposure can cause toxicity/infection.
assessment: Review transplant date/centre, baseline creatinine, immunosuppressants and timing, missed doses, new prescriptions/herbals, fever/urinary/respiratory symptoms, BP, edema, pregnancy and malignancy screening.
workup: Use creatinine/electrolytes, urinalysis/culture, drug levels and imaging/viral monitoring according to the transplant plan and syndrome.
Unexpected graft dysfunction belongs in prompt transplant-nephrology discussion rather than an outpatient watch-and-wait loop.
management: Continue immunosuppression as prescribed unless the transplant/acute-care team directs changes; treat infections with transplant-specific interaction/dose review.
Maintain vaccination, skin/cancer screening, cardiovascular risk and metabolic care according to transplant guidance.
medicationSafety: Macrolides/azoles and many other drugs/herbals can markedly change calcineurin/mTOR inhibitor levels.
Avoid live vaccines in significantly immunosuppressed transplant recipients unless a specialist pathway explicitly supports them; avoid nephrotoxins where possible.
counselling: Teach strict medication timing/adherence, interaction checking, infection precautions and early contact with the transplant team for acute illness.
followUp: Ensure lab/drug-level/cancer/vaccine surveillance and transplant-program appointments remain closed-loop.
examTrap: Stopping or reducing tacrolimus/mycophenolate independently because a transplant recipient develops an infection without contacting the transplant team.
oneLinePearl: In transplant care, protect both sides of the balance: enough immunosuppression to preserve the graft, not so much that toxicity/infection is ignored.
sourceBasis: Kidney Foundation of Canada transplant resources

title: Renal Drug Dosing: Dose to the Patient's Current Clearance and Clinical Context
bottomLine: Renal dosing is not 'reduce every drug when eGFR is low.' Determine whether the drug/active metabolite is renally cleared, which renal estimate the product/guideline uses, whether kidney function is stable or changing, and whether dialysis removes the drug; adjust dose, interval or avoid only when the pharmacology and indication require it.
recognize: Older/frail/low-muscle-mass patients can have deceptively low creatinine despite reduced kidney function.
AKI makes steady-state creatinine-based estimates less reliable because kidney function is changing faster than the equation assumes.
differentiate: eGFR indexed to 1.73 m2 and creatinine-clearance equations are not interchangeable for every drug label; use the metric required by the medication guidance.
Some drugs need loading doses despite renal impairment because loading relates to volume of distribution, while maintenance dosing depends more on clearance.
assessment: Review current and baseline creatinine/eGFR, trajectory/AKI, weight/body size, dialysis modality/timing, indication, therapeutic window, interacting nephrotoxins and medication adherence.
workup: Use current product monograph/pharmacy guidance and drug-specific monitoring; obtain serum levels when a validated therapeutic-drug-monitoring strategy exists.
Recalculate/reassess after major renal changes rather than leaving an old dose indefinitely.
management: Adjust dose/interval or choose an alternative based on renal clearance, urgency, infection/site or therapeutic target.
Coordinate dialysis timing/post-dialysis dosing for dialyzable medications and use pharmacy support for high-risk/complex regimens.
medicationSafety: Common high-risk accumulation examples include selected opioids, gabapentinoids, anticoagulants, antimicrobials and hypoglycemics; the exact adjustment remains drug-specific.
Avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins where alternatives exist and review combined nephrotoxic/hemodynamic risk during acute illness.
redFlags: Rapid AKI while receiving renally cleared narrow-therapeutic-index drugs
counselling: Teach patients with CKD to check OTC/herbal products and to report dehydration/acute illness that can change medication safety.
followUp: Review renal dosing after hospitalization, AKI recovery, dialysis changes or major weight/function change.
examTrap: Using a stable-CKD eGFR dose table unchanged during rapidly evolving AKI without reassessing the actual clinical clearance and drug toxicity risk.
oneLinePearl: Renal dosing follows the drug, the correct clearance estimate, and whether kidney function is stable today.
sourceBasis: Health Canada product monographs and Canadian renal-pharmacy practice
